She begins by extending her arms out to the sides, then raises them above her head, maintaining a fluid motion. Her movements are deliberate and precise, suggesting she is rehearsing a specific routine or dance piece. In the background, a ballet barre is visible, indicating the setting is specifically designed for dance practice. The dancer's focus and the serene environment suggest a dedicated practice session. There are no other people or significant objects in the frame, keeping the viewer's attention solely on the dancer's performance.

caption: The video captures a woman with her hair in a bun, wearing a white long-sleeved top with an open back, black flared trousers and a face mask, standing in a mirrored dance studio with her back to the camera. A ballet barre runs along the wall and a small phone rests on the floor, while her reflection fills the right side of the frame. She stands with her legs crossed in a relaxed stance. At the start her arms are bent with hands close together forming a rounded circle around her head, then rising overhead, a pose she sustains with only slight adjustments. The arms then open outward and upward into a wide raised V. They gradually lower toward her sides. As they settle, one leg extends out to the side with the foot pointed and the torso turning a little. The arms bend and draw in toward the front of her waist while the extended leg is held, with small shifts in angle, through the final frame. Her reflection reproduces each position simultaneously.

endpoints are normal, not physical errors. Do not add unseen causes, onset, stopping or outcomes.
An internal editing cut is not evidence of physical motion connecting the views.

Check identification before physical interpretation: a reflection is not a separate actor;
a powder/smoke/liquid outline or shadow is not automatically the boundary of a solid object;
an apparent change caused by occlusion/viewpoint is not automatically material deformation.
Do not claim contact, bending, compression, melting, disintegration or structural recovery unless
the appropriate material/surface itself provides visible evidence. Do not infer a force or earlier
collision just because the visible configuration would be compatible with it.

camera tracking. A single visible texture/seam does not prove spin. Avoid unnecessary absolute
claims of stillness, no motion, no camera motion or 'exactly' synchronized changes.
Remove invented scene details and explanations, but keep clearly visible ongoing motion and
processes. Avoid deleting the real process merely because its cause lies outside the cropped window.
